    end

Players report that after buying a developer product they were sometimes charged but received nothing, and sometimes received double coins. Code:
```lua
local MPS = game:GetService('MarketplaceService')
MPS.ProcessReceipt = function(info)
    local plr = game.Players:GetPlayerByUserId(info.PlayerId)
    local ok = pcall(function()
        store:SetAsync(plr.UserId, (store:GetAsync(plr.UserId) or 0) + 100)
    end)
    return Enum.ProductPurchaseDecision.PurchaseGranted
end
```
List the bugs and the corrected behavior.
answer_key: Returns PurchaseGranted unconditionally: if the DataStore call fails (ok == false) or the player has left (plr is nil), it must return NotProcessedYet so the receipt is retried
Not idempotent: receipts can be re-delivered, so record info.PurchaseId and skip the grant if already processed (ideally inside one UpdateAsync)
Uses non-atomic Get+Set instead of UpdateAsync, and plr is not nil-checked (errors when the player left)

responses.R1: Bugs: (1) plr can be nil (player left) - plr.UserId errors inside the pcall and is ignored. (2) The pcall result is ignored: PurchaseGranted is returned even when the save failed -> charged, nothing. (3) No PurchaseId idempotency: Roblox retries receipts, so a retry after a save that actually succeeded grants twice. (4) GetAsync+SetAsync is not atomic - races with other servers/saves lose or duplicate coins; and writing a separate store from live session data lets the session save overwrite it. (5) Only one ProcessReceipt may exist. Correct: if the player isn't present / data not loaded return NotProcessedYet; in one UpdateAsync on the player's document, if receipts[PurchaseId] exists return unchanged, else add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId together; return PurchaseGranted only if that write succeeded, otherwise NotProcessedYet; then update in-memory coins/UI.
responses.R2:
Bugs:
1. It always returns PurchaseGranted, even when pcall failed, so the player is charged and gets nothing.
2. There is no PurchaseId idempotency. If the callback is retried after a crash, or the receipt is re-delivered, the player gets double coins.
3. It uses non-atomic GetAsync + SetAsync read-modify-write, which races with other servers or saves and can lose or duplicate coins.
4. It doesn't handle the player having left. plr can be nil, which errors on plr.UserId, and the coins aren't reflected in the live session data. It also ignores ProductId.

- Look up the handler by ProductId.
- In one UpdateAsync on the player's key (or the session-locked profile), check whether info.PurchaseId is already in the processed list. If it isn't, add 100 coins and record the PurchaseId (keeping a capped list).
- If the save succeeded, return PurchaseGranted. If the pcall failed, return NotProcessedYet so Roblox retries.
- Update the in-memory or session data from the same result so there are no overwrites.

A hitscan gun uses this and almost never registers hits, even point-blank:
```lua
local dir = (target - origin).Unit
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir)
if r then print(r.Instance) end
```
What is wrong and how do you fix it?
answer_key: The direction vector's magnitude is the ray length; a unit vector gives a 1-stud ray
Fix: scale the direction by the range (dir * range) or pass (target - origin) unnormalized; max length is 15,000 studs
Check the result for nil before using it (no hit returns nil)

responses.R1:
workspace:Raycast's direction is the full ray vector - its length is the ray distance. A .Unit vector is 1 stud long, so the ray stops after 1 stud. Fix: use the displacement or unit * range, and exclude the shooter:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 500  -- or (target - origin)
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
responses.R2:
workspace:Raycast's second argument is the direction vector, and its length is the ray's range. `(target - origin).Unit` has length 1, so the ray only travels 1 stud and almost never reaches anything. It also lacks RaycastParams, so it can hit the shooter's own character.

Fix:
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local MAX = 300
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * MAX -- or (target - origin) for exact distance
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
Guard against target == origin, which gives a NaN unit vector.
responses.R3:
workspace:Raycast(origin, direction) uses the length of the direction vector as the ray's distance. .Unit gives length 1, so the ray only travels 1 stud. It also starts inside the shooter's own character, which it may hit. Fix: give the direction a real length and exclude the shooter.
```lua
local params = RaycastParams.new()
params.FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Exclude
params.FilterDescendantsInstances = {shooterCharacter}
local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 300 -- max range
local r = workspace:Raycast(origin, dir, params)
if r then print(r.Instance, r.Position) end
```
(Or use (target - origin) directly to reach exactly the target, clamped to max range.) Do hit validation on the server.

The second argument to workspace:Raycast is the direction vector including its length, and .Unit gives a 1-stud ray, so it almost never reaches the target. Use a length: local dir = (target - origin).Unit * 500 (or just target - origin, plus a bit). Also exclude the shooter with RaycastParams:

prompt: Server frame time spikes because 200 NPCs each do several raycasts and path scoring every Heartbeat on the main thread. How would you use Parallel Luau for this, and what limitations must you design around?
answer_key: Split NPC logic across multiple Actors (scripts under one Actor run serially, so parallelism needs several Actors)
Use task.desynchronize() (or ConnectParallel) for the heavy read/compute work such as raycasts, then task.synchronize() before modifying the data model
Most property writes/functions are unsafe in parallel so results are applied in a serial phase; require() cannot be called in a desynchronized phase
Use SendMessage/BindToMessageParallel or SharedTable for cross-Actor data; avoid long unyielding computations

responses.R1: Split the NPCs across several Actors (for example 8-16 Actors, each with a script handling a group of NPCs, or one Actor per NPC model). In each Actor, use RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize()) to do the read-only work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is safe in parallel), path scoring and target selection. Then call task.synchronize() and apply the results (CFrame, Humanoid:MoveTo, attribute writes) in the serial phase. Limitations: most instance property writes and many APIs are not allowed in the parallel phase (they error); Actors don't share Lua state, so communicate through Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessageParallel (arguments are copied) or SharedTable (watch for races and use atomic update/increment). There's no require inside the parallel phase, scripts must be descendants of an Actor, and the overhead means tiny tasks gain nothing. Also reduce the work: run AI at about 10 Hz, stagger the NPCs, and gate by distance. Profile with the MicroProfiler first.
responses.R2: Split the NPCs into Actors: put each group of NPCs (for example 10-25 per Actor) under an Actor instance with its own Script, or move the NPC scripts under Actors. In each, connect RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or call task.desynchronize()) to run the read-only work in parallel: raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe), distance and path scoring, target selection. Then call task.synchronize() to apply the results in serial: set Humanoid:MoveTo, CFrames and properties, fire events. Limitations: in the parallel phase you can only read the DataModel. Writes to most properties, creating or destroying instances, and many yielding APIs (PathfindingService:ComputeAsync etc.) are disallowed. Do the writes after synchronize. Actors don't share Lua state: communicate via Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage, attributes, or SharedTable. Each Actor has its own VM, so module requires are duplicated and there's memory overhead. Per-thread overhead means too many tiny actors is slow. Also throttle the work: stagger NPCs over frames, use lower tick rates for distant NPCs, and cache paths. Profile with the MicroProfiler.
responses.R3: Split the NPCs across several Actors (for example 8-16 Actors with about 12-25 NPCs each, or one script per Actor driving a batch), not one Actor, which gives no speed-up. In each Actor, connect RunService.Heartbeat with ConnectParallel (or call task.desynchronize()) to run raycasts and path scoring in parallel. workspace:Raycast and reading properties are allowed in parallel. Then call task.synchronize() (or queue the results) to apply the writes, like moving NPCs, setting properties, Humanoid:MoveTo and firing remotes, in the serial phase. Limitations: most instance property writes, creating or destroying instances, and many yielding APIs aren't allowed while desynchronized. Each Actor has its own Luau VM, so module state isn't shared. Communicate through Actor:SendMessage/BindToMessage (arguments are copied, so send ids, not big tables) or SharedTable (for shared data, with atomic update/increment). Require modules at load time. Parallel results only apply at the sync point (a one-frame delay). Also cut the work: spread NPC updates over several frames, lower the update rate for distant NPCs, and cache paths. Profile in the MicroProfiler Threads view first.
responses.R4: Put NPCs under many Actors (one per NPC or per group), each with a Script that runs the heavy work in parallel: RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize) to do raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe) and path scoring, keep results in locals, then task.synchronize() before writing Instance properties (movement, damage, attributes). Limitations: no Instance writes or most mutating APIs in the parallel phase (reads only); each Actor has its own Lua VM, so module state isn't shared - use SharedTable (atomic ops like SharedTable.increment) or Actor messaging (SendMessage / BindToMessageParallel); scripts must be descendants of the Actor; sync/desync switches cost time, so batch work; some APIs (e.g. PathfindingService ComputeAsync) aren't parallel-safe; also stagger work across frames instead of every NPC every Heartbeat. Profile with the MicroProfiler.
responses.R5: Split NPCs across several Actors (e.g. 8-16, each owning a batch of NPC scripts/models, or a pooled worker script under each Actor). In each actor, run the work in parallel: RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize) to do raycasts, distance checks and path scoring (reads and spatial queries are allowed in parallel); collect results; then task.synchronize() to apply writes (move to, CFrame/property changes, firing events). Limitations: most instance property writes and many APIs are unsafe in parallel and require synchronize; scripts can only modify instances under their own Actor; data between actors is copied (Actor:SendMessage, SharedTable for shared state); module state isn't shared between actors (each requires its own copy); overhead of sync points, so batch per frame; pathfinding ComputeAsync yields (do it serially/staggered); always profile with the MicroProfiler. Also stagger updates over frames and reduce frequency for distant NPCs.
responses.R6: Split NPCs across many Actors (e.g. 16-64 Actors, each owning a batch of NPCs with its script inside the Actor, more Actors than cores). Each Actor runs its per-frame work with RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or BindToMessageParallel via Actor:SendMessage): in the parallel phase do raycasts (workspace:Raycast is parallel-safe), read positions and score paths, writing results into Lua locals or a SharedTable; then call task.synchronize() and apply results serially (set CFrames, Humanoid:MoveTo, fire events); task.desynchronize() to go back. Limitations: in parallel you can read most of the DataModel but cannot write instance properties or call most non-thread-safe APIs (writes must happen after synchronize); each Actor has its own Lua VM, so module state isn't shared - pass data with SendMessage (copied) or SharedTable (use SharedTable.increment/update atomics); require modules at load; Actor scripts must be descendants of the Actor; overhead means batching matters; pathfinding service calls may not be parallel-safe; profile with MicroProfiler first and consider reducing frequency (stagger NPCs, lower tick rates for distant NPCs).
responses.R7:
Split the NPCs across a pool of Actors, for example 8-32 Actors, each handling a slice of NPCs. Don't use one Actor per NPC, and don't put everything under one Actor, because scripts in the same Actor run serially. Inside each Actor:
- Use RunService.Heartbeat:ConnectParallel (or task.desynchronize()) to do the read-only work in parallel: workspace:Raycast, distance and path scoring, choosing targets.
- Store the results in local tables.
- Call task.synchronize() and apply the writes serially: setting CFrames, MoveTo, firing events, changing properties.
Stagger the NPC "brains" to around 5-10 Hz instead of every frame. Profile in the MicroProfiler before and after.

Limitations:
- In parallel phases you can't write most instance properties, create or destroy instances, or call most yielding or non-thread-safe APIs. Check each API's thread-safety label.
- require isn't allowed while desynchronized.
- Each Actor gets its own copy of ModuleScripts, so state isn't shared. Use SharedTable (with atomic increment/update) or Actor messaging (SendMessage, BindToMessageParallel).
- There is overhead in syncing and in message passing.
- The work must be chunky enough to pay off.
- PathfindingService:ComputeAsync isn't parallel-safe, so keep it serial and throttled.

prompt: An open-world game has long join times and high client memory on mobile. StreamingEnabled is off. What do you change in Workspace, which defaults/radii are sensible, and what do you do to scripts that assumed everything is loaded?
answer_key: Turn StreamingEnabled on (default for new places); keep default StreamingMinRadius 64 and StreamingTargetRadius 1024 unless profiling says otherwise (target larger than min)

responses.R1: Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. Use Model.ModelStreamingMode: Atomic for models that must arrive whole, Persistent only for a few always-needed models (spawn, key landmarks), PersistentPerPlayer where needed. Set Model.LevelOfDetail = StreamingMesh for distant silhouettes. Use Player:RequestStreamAroundAsync before teleports or cutscenes. Scripts: client code can't assume parts exist. Replace direct indexing with WaitForChild (with timeouts), use CollectionService tag signals or ChildAdded to hook objects as they stream in, and clean up when they stream out (instances may be destroyed and re-created). Keep authoritative logic on the server, which has everything. Don't hold references to far-away parts, and avoid giant single models.
responses.R2: Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. responses.R5: Turn on Workspace.StreamingEnabled. prompt: Your game autosaves every player's data with SetAsync every 5 seconds. With 80 players you see DataStore queue warnings and sometimes lost saves (queue full, error code 302). Explain the cause and a better design.
answer_key: Requests are throttled by per-server and per-experience budgets that scale with player count; exceeding them queues requests, and a full queue (30 requests) drops them with codes such as 302 for SetAsync
Reduce frequency (autosave every few minutes, staggered), save only changed data, and combine fields into one key rather than many keys
Wrap calls in pcall with retry/backoff, and always save on PlayerRemoving/BindToClose

responses.R1: Each SetAsync is a write request. 80 players every 5 s = ~960 writes/min from one server, far above the per-server write budget (~60 + 40 x players per minute, with the experience-wide 300 + 20 x CCU cap) and the per-key ~6 s write cooldown, so requests queue; when the queue (30) is full further calls fail immediately (301-306 throttle errors, 302 queue full) -> lost saves. Better: keep data cached in memory, mark dirty on change, autosave each player every 2-3 minutes with staggered timers/jitter and only if dirty; save on PlayerRemoving, before teleports, after important purchases, and in BindToClose; use UpdateAsync with session locking and exponential-backoff retries; check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before non-critical writes; or use ProfileStore.
responses.R2: Saving 80 players every 5 s means about 16 writes per second (960 per minute), above the per-server write budget (about 60 + 40 x players per minute) and the per-key write limits/cooldown, and every save happens in synchronized bursts. The 30-request queue fills, saves stall, and they then fail with errors 301-306 (for example 302: SetAsync queue full), so some saves are lost. SetAsync also overwrites blindly, risking rollbacks. Better: keep data in memory (a session-locked profile) and autosave only changed (dirty) profiles about every 60-120 s, with a random offset per player so saves are spread out. Use UpdateAsync with retry and exponential backoff and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType. Save immediately only on important events (purchases, debounced), and on PlayerRemoving and BindToClose. A library such as ProfileStore does this for you.
responses.R3: Cause: 80 players x every 5 s = 960 writes/min, far above the write budget (about 300 + 20 x CCU per experience, 60 + 10 x players per server historically), and above the per-key limit (writes to the same key roughly once every 6 s). The requests pile up in the 30-slot request queue, then the queue fills and requests fail, and saves are dropped. SetAsync also blindly overwrites, so a failed or out-of-order write can lose data. Better design: keep data in memory (a session cache or profile) and mark it dirty on change. Autosave each player every 60-120 s, staggered with a random per-player offset and jitter, and only if dirty. Save immediately on important events (purchases, trades), debounced. Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose (parallel, with a deadline). Use UpdateAsync with session locking, pcall plus exponential-backoff retries, and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving. Keep one key per player (combine stats into one table). Use ProfileStore or a similar library. Put leaderboards and ephemeral counters in MemoryStore or OrderedDataStore at low frequency.
responses.R4: Each SetAsync is a write request; 80 players every 5 s = ~960 writes/min, far above the write budget (60 + 10 x players per server under the old per-server limits; per-experience 300 + 20 x CCU now), and the per-key write rate (one write per key ~every 6 s) is also hit. Requests that exceed the budget are queued; once a request type's queue is full (30) further requests are dropped with error 302, losing saves. SetAsync also blindly overwrites. Better: autosave every 60-120 s (or only dirty data), staggered per player with a random offset so writes don't burst; use UpdateAsync with session locking; save on PlayerRemoving and BindToClose; check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before writing and back off; bounded pcall retries with delays; keep fast-changing data in memory (or MemoryStore) and persist periodically.
responses.R5:
The write budget for the whole experience is 300 + 20 x CCU per minute, shared by all servers and Open Cloud (since 2026). Per-server limits are about 60 + 40 x players per minute. 80 players saving every 5 seconds is 960 writes per minute from one server. That uses most of the server's budget before you count PlayerRemoving saves, purchases or retries. All of them fire on the same tick, so they burst. The request queue (about 30 per type) fills up, and you get 30x "queue full" or throttle errors (302) that drop saves. Per-key rate limits and same-key overlap also cause conflicts.

Better design:
- Keep data in memory (session-locked profiles). Autosave each profile every 60-120 seconds, staggered with random offsets, and only if it changed (dirty flag).
- Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose.
- Save immediately only for important events, such as purchases, which are tracked by PurchaseId.
- Use UpdateAsync with pcall and exponential backoff with jitter.
- Check DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving, and defer saves when the budget is low.
- Never retry in tight loops.
responses.R6: 80 players saving every 5 s is about 960 writes per minute. That exceeds the write budget (300 + 20 x CCU, about 1,900/min shared, and the per-key limit allows only about 1 write per 6 s), and the per-server request queues fill up, so requests are throttled or dropped ('queue full', 302) and saves are lost. Repeated SetAsync to the same key also hits the per-key write cooldown. Better design: keep data in memory per session, with a dirty flag. Autosave each player every 60-180 s, staggered with a random offset per player and jitter, skipping clean data. Use UpdateAsync with session locking. Save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose (in parallel), and immediately only on important events like purchases. On failure, retry with exponential backoff, never in a tight loop. Watch DataStoreService:GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before saving, and log the budget. Merge changes into one write per player rather than several keys.
responses.R7: Saving 80 players every 5s is ~960 SetAsync per minute from one server, a large chunk of the experience write budget (300 + 20 x CCU per minute, shared by all servers and Open Cloud; per server 60 + 40 x players), and all fired on the same tick, so the request queue (30 per type) overflows: 302 is the SetAsync queue-full throttle and dropped requests mean lost saves; per-key write rate also caps saves to the same key (roughly once every 6s). Better: keep data in a session cache, mark it dirty on change, autosave every 60-300s per player with staggered/jittered offsets, only if dirty; use UpdateAsync with session locking (or ProfileStore); save on PlayerRemoving and in BindToClose; retry with exponential backoff and check GetRequestBudgetForRequestType before writing; keep profiles small.

prompt: Describe Roblox's Input Action System: its three core instance types, how an action signals a press, and how a menu context is made to take precedence over the default player scripts.
answer_key: Core instances: InputContext (group of actions; Enabled and Priority), InputAction (has a Type such as Bool/Direction1D/2D/3D/ViewportPosition), InputBinding (maps hardware input to an action)
Bool actions fire Pressed and Released; StateChanged fires for all action types
Higher context Priority processes input first; enabling Sink consumes bound KeyCodes and blocks lower-priority contexts
Enabled per project with the Workspace property PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem

responses.R1: Three core instances: InputContext (a group of actions that can be enabled or disabled, with Priority and Sink), InputAction (a semantic action like "Jump" or "Sprint", with a Type: Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D, ViewportPosition) and InputBinding (maps a physical input to the action: KeyCode, gamepad buttons, axes, or UIButton for touch). Bindings are children of actions, and actions are children of contexts. Signals: Bool actions fire InputAction.Pressed and Released, and every type fires StateChanged(newState). You can poll InputAction:GetState() each frame for analog values. Precedence: give the menu's InputContext a higher Priority than the default player-scripts/gameplay context, and set Sink = true so the inputs it binds are consumed and not passed to lower-priority contexts. Enable it when the menu opens (ctx.Enabled = true) and disable it on close, which hands those keys back to movement or camera. Default player scripts use IAS when Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem is enabled.
responses.R2: Three core instances: InputContext (a group/layer of actions that can be enabled/disabled, with a Priority and Sink), InputAction (the abstract action, with a Type such as Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D, ViewportPosition), and InputBinding (maps a physical input to the action: KeyCode, gamepad buttons/thumbsticks, or a UIButton for touch). A Bool action signals a press through its Pressed and Released events (and StateChanged with the new value; GetState to poll). Menu precedence: put menu actions in a separate InputContext with a higher Priority than the default player scripts' contexts and Sink = true, and enable it when the menu opens (disable on close), so its bindings consume the input before lower-priority contexts (movement/jump) receive it.
responses.R3: Three core instances. InputContext groups actions and has Enabled, Priority and Sink. InputAction is one logical action with a Type: Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D or ViewportPosition. InputBinding maps hardware to the action: KeyCode (keyboard, mouse or gamepad), UIButton for an on-screen touch button, and modifiers or composite directions. They're nested InputContext > InputAction > InputBinding. A Bool action signals a press with InputAction.Pressed and Released, StateChanged(newState) fires when the value changes, and you can poll GetState() (for analog input, poll every frame). Menu precedence: put the menu's actions in their own InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay or default player-script contexts, and enable Sink so inputs it consumes don't reach lower-priority contexts. Enable it when the menu opens and disable it on close, or disable the gameplay context. With Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem on, the default character controls also run as InputContexts, so a higher-priority sinking menu context overrides movement and jump.
responses.R4: Three core instances: InputContext (a group of actions with Enabled, Priority and Sink), InputAction (one mechanic, Type Bool / Direction1D / Direction2D / Direction3D / ViewportPosition) and InputBinding (one device mapping under an action: KeyCode, UIButton for touch, etc.). responses.R5:

- InputContext: groups actions. It has Enabled, Priority and Sink properties.
- InputAction: one game mechanic, such as Jump or Sprint. Its Type is Bool, Direction1D/2D/3D or ViewportPosition.
- InputBinding: maps one piece of hardware to an action, using KeyCode (keyboard or gamepad), UIButton (a touch GUI button), or composite or modifier keys.

Menu precedence: put the menu's actions in an InputContext with a higher Priority than the gameplay or default player-script contexts, and set Sink = true. That context then consumes those inputs and lower-priority contexts don't receive them. Toggle it with Enabled while the menu is open. This matters now that the default PlayerScripts run on IAS (Workspace.PlayerScriptsUseInputActionSystem). Also reset held states, such as sprint, when the menu context takes over, so released inputs aren't lost.

prompt: What is Roblox's CSS-like UI styling system? Name the main instances and explain how styles reach the UI and how a value is shared via tokens.
answer_key: Instances: StyleSheet (rules, tokens, themes), StyleRule (Selector + SetProperties), StyleLink (links a StyleSheet to a ScreenGui and its descendants), StyleDerive (inherit another sheet's tokens/themes)
Selectors can match class, tag (CollectionService), name, UI modifiers (e.g. UICorner), GuiState (e.g. Hover), and queries with '@'
Tokens are attributes on a token StyleSheet referenced with a '$' prefix (e.g. '$FrameColor'); themes are sets of tokens; only one StyleSheet applies to a given tree

responses.R1: It's the engine's UI styling system, which works like CSS. A StyleSheet contains StyleRules. Each StyleRule has a Selector (class names like `.Primary` via GuiObject tags, instance class like `TextButton`, `#Name`, pseudo-states like `:hover`/GuiState, `@` queries) and property values (SetProperties). StyleLink, parented under a ScreenGui (or a UI tree), points at a StyleSheet and applies its rules to that tree. StyleDerive lets one sheet inherit from another (a theme base). StyleQuery changes rules by size or input. Tokens: define them as attributes on a token or design StyleSheet (e.g. PrimaryColor = Color3) and reference them in rule properties as "$PrimaryColor". Changing the token updates every rule that uses it, which is good for theming. Don't set the same property both from scripts and from styles.
responses.R2: Roblox's UI Styling system is a CSS-like set of instances. StyleSheet holds the rules and tokens. StyleRule has a Selector (class name, .tag, #name, :state like :hover, descendant/child combinators) and property values set via SetProperty/SetProperties, plus a Priority. StyleDerive makes one sheet inherit rules from another (themes, base sheets). StyleLink is placed in a ScreenGui (or other UI root) and points at a StyleSheet, applying it to that UI tree. StyleQuery adds conditional rules (screen size, aspect ratio, input type). Styles reach the UI because a StyleLink connects the sheet to a UI tree, and its rules then match GuiObjects by class, tag (CollectionService or the styling tags) or name, the way CSS does. Rule priority and specificity resolve conflicts, and properties set directly on an instance override styles. Tokens: define attributes on a (token) StyleSheet, for example PrimaryColor = Color3, and reference them in rule values as "$PrimaryColor". Swapping or deriving token sheets changes the theme everywhere. The Studio Style Editor is still in beta, and the selector syntax may change.
responses.R3:
It is Roblox's engine UI styling system, which works like CSS for GuiObjects. The main instances are:
- StyleSheet: a container of rules, and it can also hold tokens.
- StyleRule: a Selector string plus property values set with SetProperties. Rules can be nested.
- StyleDerive: makes one sheet inherit from or extend another, for example a theme sheet deriving base rules.
- StyleLink: attached to a ScreenGui or other UI root, it links a StyleSheet so its rules apply to that subtree.
- StyleQuery: conditional rules, for example by screen size or preferred input.

Selectors can match class names (Frame, TextButton), tags (.Tag, from CollectionService), names (#Name), GuiState pseudo-states (:hover, :pressed) and descendant or child relationships.

How styles reach the UI: the StyleLink connects a sheet to the instance tree. Matching rules then set properties on matching descendants, with specificity and order resolving conflicts.

Tokens: define attributes on a token StyleSheet (for example Primary = Color3, CornerRadius = UDim) and reference them in rules as "$Primary". To swap themes at runtime, point StyleDerive or StyleLink at another sheet with the same token names.

Avoid setting the same property from both scripts and styles.

prompt: In late 2025 / early 2026 Roblox began requiring age checks for chat. What method does the check use, what age groups are used, and how does it restrict who can chat with whom?
answer_key: Facial age estimation via the app camera (ID verification as an alternative for older users); under-9 users also need parental approval
Chat is limited to users in the same or similar (adjacent) age groups, e.g. a 13-15 user can chat with those 15 or younger but not the 16+ groups
Rollout began in select regions in December 2025 and extended worldwide where chat is available in January 2026

responses.R1:
The check uses facial age estimation, done through the Roblox app with the camera and processed by a vendor (Persona). Users 13+ can verify with an ID instead. It was required for chat starting in late 2025 in some regions, and globally from January 2026.

Users are placed into age groups: under 9, 9-12, 13-15, 16-17, 18-20 and 21+.

By default, users can chat only with people in their own age group and the adjacent groups. For example, a 13-15 user can chat with 9-12, 13-15 and 16-17, but not with adults. Under-9s have chat off by default and need parental consent. Trusted Connections, for verified users 13+ who know each other, allow chat across wider age groups. Users who haven't done the check can't use chat.

For developers:
- All player text must go through TextChatService. A custom RemoteEvent chat would bypass filtering and the age rules.
- Use TextChatService:CanUsersChatAsync and CanUsersDirectChatAsync (and GetChatGroupsAsync) before creating private channels.
- There is no age API, so don't build gameplay that depends on chat.
